explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, because he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery (Isaiah 39:1). Nobody shows up with a gift for a man they don't care about. I think that's a pretty warm way to say hello.

Soldiers and a warning would be a very different kind of mail, friend. The text says Merodach-baladan sent letters and a gift (Isaiah 39:1). It gives the reason right there: he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery. No army, no threats, just a delivery.

Priests and an offering sounds solemn, but that's not what arrived. Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift (Isaiah 39:1). The text says he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery. So the package was letters and a gift.

Ohhh, close, friend, but the text says the opposite. Hezekiah showed them the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil and his entire armory, all that was found in his storehouses. Then it adds, "There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them." (Isaiah 39:2) A few treasures? He showed them the whole building.

That's right, friend. It was not a few treasures. Hezekiah showed them the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil and his entire armory (Isaiah 39:2). The text says there was "nothing in his palace or in all his dominion" that he did not show them. When I show somebody my bakery, I at least keep one cookie jar closed.

That's the word, friend. Isaiah says the LORD declares that everything in the palace, and all that Hezekiah's fathers had stored up until that day, "will be carried off to Babylon." Then comes the line, "Nothing will be left, says the LORD." (Isaiah 39:6) The visitors who got the grand tour were from the very place it would go.

No fire in this word, friend. The LORD says it will be "carried off to Babylon" (Isaiah 39:6). Carried off means moved, not burned. I know a great fire is the dramatic guess, but I'd rather lose a batch to the oven than guess past what the text says.

Good guess, friend, but the text names a different place. The word of the LORD says everything will be "carried off to Babylon." (Isaiah 39:6) Babylon is the very land the envoys came from (Isaiah 39:3). So the answer was sitting in Hezekiah's own conversation.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." (Isaiah 39:7) This part is heavy, so we won't joke about it. It goes beyond the treasure, and it reaches Hezekiah's own family line.

I see why you'd go there, friend, since Hezekiah had that whole armory on display. But the word of the LORD names his descendants: "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood." (Isaiah 39:7) That means his own family line, not his troops. It's a heavy part, and I think it's meant to land that way.

Advisers is a fair thought, friend, but it's not what the text says. The word of the LORD says "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." (Isaiah 39:7) It names Hezekiah's own family. That's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up.

That's what he said, friend. Hezekiah answered Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (Isaiah 39:8) It's a surprising thing to say after such news. The very next card shows what the text says he was thinking.

I'd expect that too, friend. If somebody told me my family's future was heading to another land, I'd have a lot to say. But Hezekiah said, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (Isaiah 39:8) He didn't call it harsh, so we don't either.

That would be the arguing answer, friend, and Hezekiah didn't argue. He said, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (Isaiah 39:8) No pushing back at all. What he said next is its own surprise.

explanations.answer: At least his own lifetime will have peace
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, "For he thought, 'At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.'" (Isaiah 39:8) That's Hezekiah's own thought, and it's right there in the verse. I think it's a quiet, sad note to end on. But the story isn't over for Hezekiah's land, so keep listening.

explanations.answer: Babylon will soon forget all about Judah
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but Hezekiah's thought wasn't about Babylon forgetting anything. The text says, "At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime." (Isaiah 39:8) His mind went to his own lifetime. That's the thought the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: Isaiah could still turn out to be mistaken
explanations.explanation: That would be a hopeful way out, friend, but it's not in the text. Hezekiah called the word good, and then "he thought, 'At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.'" (Isaiah 39:8) Nothing there says he doubted Isaiah. The thought was about peace in his own days.
